A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

sensory rhodopsins I and II have the same mechanism for signal transduction, namely a light-driven conformational change in the receptor, but the conformational change is opposite and the direction of signaling is reversed.

we have shown that two forms of sensory rhodopsins I are directly correlated with attract and repellent phototaxis signals, and that opposite displacements of the helix F in the two conformers correspond to opposite phototaxis signal.
sensory rhodopsins have evolved to use different mechanisms for the same purpose: to transduce light energy into a signal that is used for phototaxis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sensory rhodopins are not just light-driven pumps but are light-driven signaling proteins that can be tuned to different signaling states by light-induced conformational changes.
sensory rhodopsins are not just a family of proteins that sense light but rather are proteins that are capable of sensing and responding to light in a variety of different ways.
sensory rhodopsins, and by implication other members of the rhodopsin family of proteins, can have multiple conformations that differ in their ability to activate or inhibit the histidine kinase.
